title: Virtual environments
objective: Explain why every project gets its own virtual environment, and write the commands to create one, switch it on, and save its packages.

explanation.text: This lesson is about your own computer, so the commands have a Copy button and cannot run in the browser. The exercises still check your understanding, with small Python functions that build and read the commands.

Different projects need different packages, and sometimes different **versions** of the same package. If you install everything into one place, projects start to break each other. A **virtual environment** (venv) is a private folder of packages for one project.

explanation.title: make and use a virtual environment (Windows)
explanation.text: Run these in the project folder. The first line makes the folder .venv. Use copies of nothing: a venv only holds packages.
explanation.code:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install requests
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
deactivate

explanation.title: the same on macOS or Linux
explanation.text: Only the activate line is different.
explanation.code:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install requests
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
deactivate

explanation.text: In Windows PowerShell the activate line is `.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`. If PowerShell says scripts are disabled, run `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned` once, or use the Command Prompt instead.
To rebuild the same environment on another computer, make a new venv, activate it, and run `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`.

walkthrough.title: The venv workflow
walkthrough.code:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install requests
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
deactivate

lines.explain: Runs the `venv` module and makes a folder called `.venv` with its own copy of Python and an empty package list.
Switches the environment on for this terminal. Your prompt usually shows `(.venv)`. From now on `python` and `pip` use the venv.
Installs the package into the venv, not into your whole computer. `python -m pip` makes sure that pip belongs to the same Python.
Writes every installed package and its exact version into a text file. `>` sends the output into the file.
Switches the environment off. The terminal goes back to normal.

exercises.prompt: Write `create_command(folder)`. It returns the command that makes a virtual environment in that folder, such as `python -m venv .venv`.
hints: It is text: `python -m venv` and then the folder name.

exercises.prompt: Write `activate_command(folder, system)`. For `"windows"` return `FOLDER\Scripts\activate`. For `"mac"` or `"linux"` return `source FOLDER/bin/activate`. For any other system return `None`.
hints: In Python text, a backslash is written twice: `"\\"`.

exercises.prompt: Write `parse_requirements(text)`. Each useful line of a `requirements.txt` is a package name followed by an optional version rule, like `requests==2.32.4` or `pytest>=8`. Return a list of `(name, rule)` pairs in order. The rule is everything after the name (an empty string when there is none). Skip empty lines and lines that start with `#`.

debug.title: A requirements file with comments
debug.symptom: ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)
debug.prompt: This function should return a dictionary of the **pinned** packages (lines like `name==version`). It crashes on comments, blank lines and unpinned packages. Fix it: ignore every line that is not `name==version`.
hints: An empty line or a comment has no `==`, so `split("==")` gives one piece, not two.
Check `"==" in line` and that the line does not start with `#` before you split.

mistakes.mistake: Installing packages without activating the environment first.
mistakes.why: They go into your global Python, not the project.
mistakes.fix: Look for `(.venv)` in your prompt before you run `pip`.

mistakes.why: It is big, it is different on every computer, and `requirements.txt` already describes it.

mistakes.mistake: Running a bare `pip` that belongs to a different Python.
mistakes.why: The package lands in a place your script does not look.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to save `requirements.txt` after installing something.
mistakes.why: Nobody else (and not you next year) can rebuild the same environment.
mistakes.fix: Run `python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt` after you change packages.

quiz.question: Why does each project get its own virtual environment?
options: So projects cannot break each other with different package versions
Because Python only allows one project
quiz.explanation: Each project can have exactly the packages and versions it needs.

quiz.question: What does `deactivate` do?
options: Switches the environment off for this terminal
quiz.explanation: The folder stays. Only your terminal stops using it.

quiz.question: Why use `python -m pip` and not just `pip`?
options: It makes sure pip belongs to the same Python you are using
quiz.explanation: Then the package is installed for the Python that will run your script.

challenge.title: A safe .gitignore
challenge.prompt: Write `missing_ignores(text)`. `text` is the content of a `.gitignore` file. Return the entries from `[".venv/", "__pycache__/", ".env"]` that are **not** in it (a line must match exactly after removing spaces at the ends). Keep that order.
challenge.stretch: Also accept `.venv` (without the slash) as a match for `.venv/`.
hints: Make a set of the stripped lines of `text`.
Loop over the three wanted entries and keep the ones that are not in the set.
